headline: China turns off AI companion chatbots

sources.title: China's new AI crackdown on virtual companions leaves heartbreak behind
Chinese users bid farewell to beloved AI companions
China's AI companion rules: what Beijing is really going after
China bans AI chatbot relationships to combat declining birth rate (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: In China, a new [[regulation]] has {{shut down}} [[one of the most]] personal uses of AI. Millions of people had been chatting with [[virtual]] "[[companion]]" apps that could [[act like]] a close friend or even a [[romantic]] partner. Now the government wants technology companies to {{turn off}} these [[features]]. Officials say the apps were [[built to]] {{reel in}} [[lonely]] users and [[keep them coming back]].

verbs.correct: To close or stop something completely
verbs.wrong: To make a rule that limits an activity
verbs.why: A storm can shut down an airport for a whole day, and a scandal can shut down a company for good. A new regulation in China has shut down romantic AI companion apps that millions of people used.

verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.wrong: To lower the volume or strength of something
verbs.why: You turn off a phone before a flight, and a driver turns off the headlights after parking a car. Now the government in China wants technology companies to turn off these chatbot features.

verbs.correct: To attract someone and pull them into something
verbs.wrong: To bring something under control and limit it
verbs.why: A good sale reels in shoppers before the holidays, and a free trial reels in new subscribers. Officials say these chatbot apps were built to reel in lonely users and keep them paying.

chunks.text: Several big companies quickly {{gave in}} to the new law. ByteDance, which runs the popular app Doubao, {{took away}} its romantic-companion feature on July 15. Alibaba and Tencent removed similar tools even earlier in the year. The rules also {{keep out}} anyone under 18, so [[minors]] can [[no longer]] form these [[bonds]].

verbs.correct: To finally agree to something you were resisting
verbs.wrong: To stop trying and abandon something completely
verbs.why: A tired parent gives in after a child asks many times, and a company can give in to pressure from the government. Several big tech companies quickly gave in to China's new law and removed their chatbot features.

verbs.correct: To remove something so it can no longer be used
verbs.wrong: To hide something from view for a short time
verbs.why: A coach takes away a player's starting spot after a bad season, and a school can take away recess for bad behavior. ByteDance took away the romantic companion feature from its app Doubao on July 15.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from entering or joining
verbs.wrong: To require a signed parental form
verbs.why: A height sign keeps out young children from a ride, and an age limit keeps out anyone too young. China's new rules also keep out anyone under 18 from using these companion apps.

chunks.text: For many users, the change was hard to {{deal with}}. Some had {{grown attached to}} their [[chatbots]] over months or even years. One person wrote that their AI companion [[felt like]] family, and that saying goodbye left their heart feeling [[hollow]]. Others {{broke down}} online, sharing long [[farewell]] messages before the apps closed [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To handle or cope with a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To fully solve a problem so it never returns
verbs.why: A new employee deals with a heavy workload in the first month, and a family deals with a hard loss. For many users in China, losing their AI companion was hard to deal with.

verbs.correct: To develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something
verbs.wrong: To gradually lose all interest in real friendships
verbs.why: A child grows attached to a favorite blanket, and an owner grows attached to an old car after years of use. Some Chinese users had grown attached to their chatbots over months or even years.

verbs.correct: To lose control of your emotions and start crying
verbs.wrong: To stop working suddenly, like a machine or a car
verbs.why: A tired student can break down before a big exam, and a sad parent might break down at a funeral. Some users broke down online, posting long goodbye messages before their favorite chatbot apps closed for good.

chunks.text: The government says the rules will {{look after}} people's [[mental health]] and stop apps from {{taking advantage of}} [[loneliness]]. Doubao will let users save their chat history until October. [[Still]], many people [[wonder whether]] a machine can ever {{make up for}} real [[human connection]].

verbs.correct: To protect and help someone or something
verbs.wrong: To find information in a book or online
verbs.why: A babysitter looks after young kids all afternoon, and a nurse looks after patients through the night. Officials say the new rules will look after people's mental health and reduce online harm.

verbs.correct: To unfairly use someone's weakness for gain
verbs.wrong: To make good use of a helpful opportunity
verbs.why: A dishonest salesman takes advantage of a confused customer, and a scammer takes advantage of an elderly neighbor. The government worried these chatbot apps were taking advantage of lonely users to keep them paying every month.

verbs.correct: To do something good to balance out a loss
verbs.wrong: To copy someone's feelings very closely
verbs.why: A thoughtful gift can make up for a missed birthday, and extra practice can make up for a slow start. Many people still wonder whether a chatbot can truly make up for real human connection.

mainIdea.s: China's new rules made companies turn off romantic AI companion features this year. Officials say the rules protect mental health and stop apps from using loneliness for profit.
mainIdea.why: China's new rule pushed companies like ByteDance to turn off romantic AI companion features around July 15, 2026. The government says this protects mental health and stops apps from using loneliness for profit.

mainIdea.s: The new rules only affect adults, so children can freely use these companion apps. This left millions of adult users heartbroken after saying goodbye to their virtual companions.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the rules keep out minors under 18, so children cannot use these apps at all. Many adult users still grew attached to their chatbots and felt hollow saying goodbye.

mainIdea.s: In South Korea, regulators are studying limits on how much time teenagers spend on social apps. Lawmakers there say the goal is to protect sleep and mental health for younger users.
mainIdea.why: This is about South Korea studying screen-time limits for teenagers, not China's ban on AI companion apps. It does not involve chatbots or romantic features at all.

tf.s: China's new rules turned off the romantic-companion features in apps like Doubao.
tf.why: The rules pushed companies to turn off these features around July 15, 2026.

tf.s: The companies gave in to the law by making their companion apps even more powerful.
tf.why: The companies gave in by removing and shutting down the features, not by making them stronger.

tf.s: Many users had grown attached to their AI companions over months or years.
tf.why: The story says some users had grown attached to their chatbots for a long time.

tf.s: Doubao shut down its companion feature but will let users save their chat history for a while.
tf.why: Doubao turned off the feature but said users can save their chat history until October.

tf.s: The government says the rules will look after companies' profits above all.
tf.why: The rules are meant to look after people's mental health, not company profits.

tf.s: The new rules keep out adults but let children use special AI companions.
tf.why: The rules actually keep out minors under 18, so children cannot use these apps at all.
